title: Water-heater integral action in isolation
physicalPurpose: Adjust heater power until persistent outlet-temperature error disappears after a constant load change.
objective: Calculate the integral heater-output change per scan, then use an equivalent load experiment to explain why integral action removes constant-load offset but gives a slower transient response on its own.

simplifications: The recirculating volume is one well-mixed thermal state.
Applied heater power equals the bounded integral contribution because Kp, Kd, feedforward, and bias are zero.
The constant load event changes the zero-power equilibrium by 3 degC.

baseline.limitation: The Lesson 5 baseline retains 1.15 degC changed-load mean absolute error because fixed bias cannot adapt.

change.decision: Isolate integral action from the same measured holding output so offset removal and slower early-load correction are compared directly.

abortPredicates: PV or MV leaves its hard limit
simulationOnlyRestrictions: The integral-only experiment is simulation evidence and is not a recommended physical heater controller.

video.viewerOutcome: Calculate an integral increment and use qualified evidence to explain why integral memory removes constant-load offset but is not selected alone.

learning.context: The same recirculating water heater uses a one-sided 0-to-100-percent element to hold 35 degrees Celsius while cold-water flow changes.
learning.reason: Lesson 5 retained 1.15 degrees Celsius changed-load error because fixed bias could not discover the changed holding output.
theory: The setpoint (SP) is the desired outlet-water temperature and the process value (PV) is the measured outlet-water temperature; both use degrees Celsius.
The error (e) is the setpoint minus the process value in degrees Celsius.
The requested manipulated variable (MV_requested) is calculated before limits and the applied manipulated variable (MV_applied) is the bounded heater command.
The integral contribution (uI) changes and stores heater power for as long as an error persists.
The integral gain (Ki) is the percentage-point command change per degree Celsius-second of error.
The cycle time (dt) is the seconds between updates, and the integral contribution (uI) is the stored part of the heater command.
After those quantities are defined, the per-scan relationship is uI,new = uI,old + Ki multiplied by e multiplied by dt.
A constant error creates a ramp, while zero error leaves the stored command unchanged.
Integral action has no immediate proportional correction and adds dynamic lag, so integral-only control is slower and can oscillate.
learning.workedPrediction: A 2 degree Celsius error with integral gain 0.5 percentage point per degree Celsius-second and cycle time 0.1 second adds 0.10 percentage point per scan and 1.0 percentage point over ten unchanged-error scans.
practicalPreparation: Start disabled, command the measured 75 percent holding output in bounded Manual operation, and qualify the 35 degree Celsius operating point before Auto.
Keep the plant, event at 60 seconds, 0.1-second interval, duration, limits and seed equal, then retain a zero-output Manual restoration for each case.
learning.baseline: Run the Lesson 5 proportional-gain-8, measured-bias-75 controller from the qualified operating point.
learning.change: Repeat from the same operating point with integral gain 0.5, zero proportional and derivative gains, zero bias, and the measured holding output preloaded at transfer.
learning.comparison: Before results, define final-window settling, early and final mean absolute error, cumulative applied-output movement, requested/applied ranges, validity and simulation-only criteria.
learning.validation: Verify both final windows are settled, integral final error is at most 0.2 degrees Celsius, early-load error and actuator movement expose the transient cost, all signals are bounded, and both runs restore safely.
learning.explanation: The stored integral contribution reaches the changed holding output at zero error, while accumulated rather than immediate correction explains the larger early-load error and movement.
learning.transfer: Apply the same reasoning to another self-regulating process, but recognize an integrating plant as a boundary; Lesson 7 combines prompt proportional correction with stored integral action.
